Series::hardshrink¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series::hardshrink() const -> Series
Series::hardshrink(double lambd) const -> Series

What It Does¶

hardshrink() zeroes every value whose magnitude is within a threshold and passes the rest through unchanged:

hardshrink(x) = x   if |x| > lambda
              = 0   if |x| <= lambda

The default lambda is 0.5. It is a hard “dead zone” around the origin — a denoising / sparsifying step that removes small-magnitude coefficients (in a wavelet shrinkage sense) while leaving large ones exactly as they were.

Unlike the shrinkage variant that also subtracts lambda from the survivors, hardshrink() does not shift the values it keeps.

An integer input is promoted to a floating-point result; a float32 input stays float32.

Parameters¶

lambd (double, optional)

The half-width of the dead zone. Defaults to 0.5. The comparison uses |x| > lambda, so a value exactly at +/-lambda is zeroed. Negative lambd is treated as its absolute value.

Returns¶

Series The shrunk values, same shape as the input.

Gradient¶

hardshrink() is differentiable. Its backward is a straight-through gate:

d/dx hardshrink(x) = 1   if |x| > lambda
                   = 0   if |x| <= lambda

Outside the dead zone the value is passed through untouched, so the gradient is 1; inside, the output is a constant 0, so the gradient is 0.

Examples¶

Example 1. The default lambda = 0.5 dead zone.

pluss::series::print(
    std::cout,
    pluss::make_series({-2.0, -0.3, 0.3, 2.0}).hardshrink());

Output¶

Series(shape=[4], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[-2.0000, 0.0000, 0.0000, 2.0000]

-0.3 and 0.3 are within 0.5 of zero, so they are removed; -2 and 2 pass through unchanged.

Example 2. A wider threshold removes more.

pluss::series::print(
    std::cout,
    pluss::make_series({-2.0, -0.7, 0.7, 2.0}).hardshrink(1.0));

Output¶

Series(shape=[4], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[-2.0000, 0.0000, 0.0000, 2.0000]

With lambda = 1.0, +/-0.7 now falls inside the dead zone.

Example 3. The backward is 1 outside the dead zone and 0 inside — a straight-through gate.

auto x = pluss::make_series({-2.0, -0.3, 0.3, 2.0});
x.tracks_slope_(true);

x.hardshrink().sum().reverse();

pluss::series::print(std::cout, x.sensitivity());

Output¶

Series(shape=[4], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[1.0000, 0.0000, 0.0000, 1.0000]

Example 4. float32 in, float32 out.

pluss::series::print(
    std::cout,
    pluss::make_series({-2.0f, 0.3f, 2.0f}, pluss::ScalarType::Float32).hardshrink());

Output¶

Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float32, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[-2.0000, 0.0000, 0.0000]

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • The dead-zone test is strict on the outside (|x| > lambda), so a value exactly at +/-lambda is zeroed.

  • hardshrink() keeps survivors unchanged; it does not subtract lambda from them.

  • Integer input is promoted to floating point.

Summary¶

hardshrink(x, lambda) is a hard dead zone around the origin:

  • 0 for |x| <= lambda (default 0.5), x unchanged otherwise

  • promotes integer input; keeps float32

  • differentiable: straight-through gradient 1 outside the dead zone, 0 inside

See Also¶

  • Series::relu: a one-sided hard gate rather than a symmetric dead zone.

  • Series::clamp_min / Series::clamp_max: for bounding magnitudes instead of zeroing small ones.
